1:
Keil and Delitzsch set out the chapter before expounding it: an introduction fixing time and circumstances, the purchase of a hereditary field executed in full legal form with its meaning attached, a prayer asking how that purchase could be reconciled with the surrender of the people, the Lord's reply that he will certainly give up the city because Israel and Judah have roused his wrath, and finally that he will gather them again out of every land. Clarke divides it likewise.

Where and why the prophet was confined Ellicott reconstructs. Six years have passed since the earlier prophecy; the king's intriguing policy had provoked the siege in his ninth year, and being irritated by continued predictions of defeat he put the prophet in the dungeon for state-prisoners at the palace. Two later chapters, both earlier in date, show he had been kept in a scribe's house as a private prison and was moved so the king might consult him on the siege's issue; he could not leave, but friends had access. Calvin makes the confinement the point: though he was shut up, the word of God was not bound, and he was no less free than if he had walked the streets, for heavenly truth cannot be stopped however the world rages against its ministers.

The arithmetic of the siege three work out. Gill dates its beginning to the tenth day of the tenth month of the ninth year. Clarke reckons it began the year before this word came and ran a year after, ending in the fifth month, about eighteen months and twenty-seven days in all. Calvin has the army come up near the end of the ninth year, two months of siege that year, the vision in the tenth, and a year and a half in all. Henry adds the temper of both sides, besiegers pressing with vigour and besieged resolved to hold out to the last extremity, and observes that judgments came gradually, and only because they would not meet God by repentance did he proceed until all lay waste.

Why the king took it so ill Calvin explains twice. The prophet had spoken not only of the ruin of the city but of the fall of the king, and we know how delicate kings' ears are; but he should have been softened on finding the oracle came from God, and keeping him in prison still proves his stupidity. The second reason is generic: kings seek exemption from all laws, and while allowing the people to be reproved wish themselves held sacred, so that classing the king with the commons was not to be endured. Calvin also proposes reading the four verses after the first as a parenthesis reciting circumstances.

Clarke reads the promised interview as a picture of servitude: to speak mouth to mouth and have one's eyes meet the conqueror's is the posture of abject slavery, a slave being obliged to fix his eyes on every motion of a master who often gave his orders only by dumb signs.

The last clause is ambiguous and divides them. Ellicott says the word is used elsewhere both of punishing and of delivering, prefers the second on an earlier chapter's usage, and thinks the prophet looks for a general mitigation for the exiles and hopes, without predicting it, that the king would not be excluded; nothing is known of him afterwards, though the absence of his name when the other king was released suggests he was dead by then. Calvin reports the reading that makes the visitation his death, probable at first sight since his condition was never improved as the other king's was, and then inclines the other way, that some alleviation was promised, if a certain kind of death may be called a favour, for he was not slain with the sword. Wesley says simply, perhaps in mercy.
6:
Whether this was vision or transaction Calvin settles from the context: some thought the Spirit merely exhibited it, but the cousin came in person and the field was bought before witnesses. Gill draws out what the forewarning proves: the visit was contingent as second causes go, yet announced as certain, so such events are foreknown and sure to God, and the man came freely, the decree not infringing free will. Ellicott finds the lesson on the surface: with ruin and exile certain, the prophet gives practical proof that he is as sure of the return.

Why the seller wanted rid of it nobody says. Ellicott guesses the village lay ravaged, the field an inheritance of ruin its owner would take any price for; or that, the prophet having urged submission, the title was safer in hands the invaders would spare, the seller staying on as his representative. Clarke states the law behind it: family estates were never to be alienated, so a man forced by poverty to sell offered first to his nearest kinsman, who might redeem what had gone to a stranger. Since priestly land could not be sold, Ellicott supposes it came in by marriage, or that transfer within the family was tolerated.

The price puzzles them. Ellicott sets it against the four hundred paid for a burial cave, the fifty for a threshing floor, the thirty for a potter's ground, and finds it far under value, so that the act falls short of its Roman parallel, where a man bought land at full price while an invading army marched on the gate. The odd phrasing, seven shekels and ten, he takes for conveyancing formula, and asks whether the numbers were picked because multiplied they give the years of captivity — an artifice in character for a writer who used acrostics and a cypher alphabet. Calvin reaches the smallness differently: Levites held no farmland, only a suburban meadow for a cow or two, and the sum proves this such a plot. Clarke notes that money was weighed, not counted, because none was yet coined, and Wesley that prices had strangely fallen with the enemy at the capital.

Keil and Delitzsch stress that the conveyance was completed in full legal form — written, sealed, witnessed, the silver weighed on the balance as still in the East — and that the sealing is not a signature but a closing up, since two copies were made, one sealed and one open, so that if the open one were defaced a perfect original survived. Clarke adds that both copies went into the jar only because the city was about to burn; deeds lodged as usual would have perished. Ellicott thinks the open copy held matter not concerning the witnesses — the price, the terms of resumption, perhaps the seventy years — Wesley that it was for the judges to ratify.

Calvin defends the confession that the prophet then knew the word was the Lord's. He had not doubted it; but revealed and experimental knowledge differ, and when the event seals the vision nothing is taken from the credit of the word, for God has regard to weakness, and the harmony of promise with fulfilment confirms others. Calvin also wants the disputed noun rendered roll rather than evidence, and would repunctuate so the sealing follows the witnessing and weighing rather than preceding them.

The jar and the long wait close the sign. Ellicott recalls that earthen vessels held a household's treasures, safer from damp than wood, and hears in the many days a warning that deliverance, however certain, would not be quick. Calvin says the same from the other side: the deed was to outlive its witnesses, for we must not measure God's faithfulness by our own lifespan. Clarke reads it more hopefully — the young, all under ten, might live to fourscore and reoccupy the ground themselves.
16:
Gill notices the order: the deeds were handed over first, and only then did the prophet pray, teaching that a soul entering religious duty should be quit of worldly concern. Henry finds the same hint and states the occasion — the two purposes disclosed to him, to pull the nation down and in time build it up, puzzled the man who had faithfully delivered both and could not reconcile them, so he poured out his soul and eased himself. What troubled him was not the bad bargain he had made for himself but the case of his people, for whom he remained a kind intercessor, hoping that so much mercy in store hereafter meant less severity now.

Calvin takes the confession of perplexity as evidence about prophecy itself. God's counsel was not disclosed to prophets entire, only so far as was expedient; yet they were not seized with ecstasies like heathen soothsayers who claimed to be carried beyond their senses, nor did they sound like brass or like the beast that rebuked its rider. They were disciples, passing on as from hand to hand what had been committed to them, and their knowledge was compatible with ignorance of much. Here the promise was plain and the sign no obscure riddle; the reason stayed hidden, and that drove him to pray.

Clarke can hardly get past his admiration. Weight of matter, sublimity of expression, profound veneration, divine unction, powerful pleading and strength of faith; historical without flatness, condensed without obscurity, confessing the worst of crimes against the most righteous of Beings neither despairing of mercy nor presuming on goodness. Ellicott places it more soberly: the prophet records his own praying, and outside the confessions of the scribe, the sick king and the exile the older Scriptures offer no such specimen of how a devout Israelite opened his heart, dwelling on the divine attributes, praying for himself and interceding for his nation.

The opening looks incoherent, Calvin admits, until one sees what it is for. Knowing how much liberty men take when they discuss God's works, the prophet bridles himself before reaching his subject: it does not become me to contend with thee or to demand a reason for thy doings. Under it lies a contrast between God and mortal man — who am I to summon thee to a contest, when heaven above and earth below are alike full of a power we are right to dread? Ellicott adds that the confession of omnipotence is everywhere the ground of prayer, an axiom of the faith since patriarchal times, and that the chapter repeats it.

Mercy and retribution are held together. Gill reads the thousands as generations, not persons, and says the clause was needed, since omnipotence proves only that nothing is beyond God, not that he will act graciously here; kindness experienced by multitudes through every age is what grounds hope. Ellicott hears an echo of the commandments and more of the proclamation of the divine glory, and finds both a righteous retribution working through the seeming injustice that runs with the continuity of family and national life — the thing the sour-grapes proverb had caricatured — and a mercy wider than it and finally triumphant.

Keil and Delitzsch sum the last clauses as greatness shown twice over, in the wisdom that watches what men do and in the power that carries out what has been decreed, so that each is repaid by his own deeds. Calvin distinguishes counsel from execution: the wisdom itself not merely surpasses our thoughts but swallows them, and would be wholly unknown were it not made visible in works, while the open eyes mean a providence reaching every corner, from which nothing is hidden and no one escapes. Clarke compresses it to omniscience and omnipresence, and Ellicott hears the note of individual recompense, which no inherited good or evil contradicts.
20:
In what sense the wonders done in Egypt lasted until that day is the first quarrel. Calvin and Wesley take it of memory: God did not work miracles in every age, but these deserved perpetual remembrance, and were still spoken of. Ellicott allows that reports of frogs and lice and boils might have looked to the prophet like a partial continuance, but settles for effect and reputation — the name outlived the signs. Keil and Delitzsch reject both readings, and Jerome's attempt to attach the phrase to what follows as well; grammatically the words belong to the verb, in a pregnant construction paralleled earlier in the book. Ellicott also strikes out the word other, which the Hebrew lacks, leaving a claim of government over mankind at large.

Gill dwells on the plagues themselves as public facts. They were set among the Egyptians, true and obvious, open to the senses, admitting no deception, and the tradition of them was still current in that nation centuries later. But he will not have physical traces surviving: that the tracks of the royal chariot wheels could still be seen in the sea bed is to be rejected as fabulous, whatever historian repeats it.

Why so much display, Calvin asks, if not to prove a father's care for his chosen and confirm the covenant with them; the miracles commend mercy at least as much as power. Gill adds that the deliverance had been promised to the patriarch centuries before, that a peculiar people were nonetheless slaves, and that they could not free themselves, since the oppressor would not let them go until compelled by a stronger hand. Calvin makes the same point from the other end: without an unmistakable display the people might have credited their escape to themselves or to some worldly instrument.

Then the land, and the ingratitude. Gill notes the oath kept, and a country that was pure gift rather than desert, granted by one with the right to dispose of it and taken from earlier holders for their wickedness. Calvin says its fruitfulness doubles the debt: a people already more than bound was bound again by wealth, and to bury both benefits was baseness. He also refuses Jerome's escape, that the fathers had merit though the children had none. And ignorance was no plea, since they could not eat a crumb without being reminded whose expulsion of the nations had given it. Keil and Delitzsch put it flatly: wonders of grace requited with unthankfulness, the commandments answered by their opposite.

The siege works before the walls draw four descriptions. Gill offers ramparts or batteries thrown up to annoy the place, and reports that some read engines for casting stones and others rams for breaching. Clarke sees huge terraces raised so that missiles could be thrown in, and infers from the siege running most of another year that the defence was a noble one. Ellicott prefers mounds to mounts and identifies them with the banks and wooden towers that were the chief instrument of ancient siegecraft. Wesley takes them for the engines rather than the earthworks.

Only now, Calvin observes, does the prophet let his difficulty out. The long preface was a bridle, since thoughts unrestrained turn petulant toward God; having set the immeasurable power before himself, and granted the justice of the vengeance, he can ask how a field was to be bought while city and country were being handed to the enemy. He confesses himself embarrassed, yet the obedience came first and without delay. Ellicott hears the ending as deliberate: the ray came when the dark was thickest, and the order was so strange and the hope so improbable that he simply leaves the whole matter where it belongs.
26:
Henry reads the reply as a lesson in singing of mercy and judgment at once. The prophet could not make the two words agree; he is told both are true, both pure, both will be made good, and not a syllable of either falls. He had allowed himself to hope the purchase meant the sentence revoked and the siege lifted, and is corrected: assurances of future mercy are no security against present trouble. Nor is the mercy merely the recovery of ground: the fields are a figure of spiritual blessings worth incomparably more, so that this oracle holds threatenings and promises as heavy as any in the older Scriptures.

The answer opens by echoing the prayer, which Ellicott takes as the prophet's vindication: he had not been wrong to throw himself on a loving omnipotence, and the phrase he used was more to him than a formula. Calvin notes that the verb can mean hidden as well as wonderful, so that some read it of nothing escaping notice; he prefers power, since anxiety comes of obstacles that cost God no labour to pass. Gill hears in the title of all flesh both weakness and corruption — unable to resist the divine will, unworthy of favour — and takes the opening call for attention as antidote to doubt. Henry adds that one who is God of all flesh could raise a people to his name out of any other nation.

Calvin insists the reply has two parts aimed at two audiences. Vengeance comes first, to terrify despisers of the law and shut them out of the coming favour, because hypocrites were already claiming the promise of restoration without faith or repentance; the mitigation that follows is meant for the elect alone, who are the only ones capable of receiving it. The two halves look contrary and are not.

On the sentence itself Gill prefers to say the besiegers will enter rather than come, since they were already at the walls, battering, shooting, cutting down whoever came within reach. Calvin asks why the word city is repeated so insistently and answers from the confidence it was breaking: being sanctuary and royal seat, the place was thought impregnable, the sun likelier to fall than its walls; so the name is driven home with the promise that not a stone would stand until the time of restoring.

The rooftops carry the sharpest irony. Clarke supposes the deity honoured there was the sun, which is why the flat parapeted roofs were chosen for incense at his rising while he stood above the horizon. Ellicott lets the judgment fall on the very spots that had been turned from true worship, so that the smoke of the false offering ends as the smoke of burning beams. Henry presses the effrontery: the thing was done not in corners, as men do who are ashamed, but in the open, with no pleasure or profit to be had by it, purely to try a jealousy they knew was there and dare it to its face.

The last verse widens the charge, and the naming needs care. Ellicott finds the same phrase used twice over with different reach, first of the northern kingdom set against Judah, then of the whole undivided nation, and hears the closing words repeat a warning from the law. Calvin makes it a rule: joined with Judah the name means the ten tribes, standing alone it takes in every child of the patriarch. He adds that the southern kingdom, preserved for a while when the north had already left the pure worship, is the more guilty for falling in with them at last. Clarke calls them transgressors from their earliest history, idolaters beyond others, worshipping what their own hands had made; Gill notes that survivors of the ten tribes were by then mixed among Judah and Benjamin.
31:
Dating the offence from the founding of the city sends Ellicott back to the united monarchy. Even then, he thinks, the place fell short of the holiness its royal founder had sought for it in the psalms of ascent, and had been to its God nothing but anger and fury; there is no Hebrew word behind the rendering provocation. He notes too that the prophet speaks as though Israel built the place, forgetting the older inhabitants dispossessed there — an oversight he excuses, since the enlargement after the capture was so thorough that the description is nearly literal.

Calvin uses the same clause to forestall a complaint. Burning a capital and levelling a sanctuary is a dreadful sentence, and many would call it excessive; the answer is that the iniquity had reached its highest pitch, so the severity kept within due measure. He rejects the version that has the city reduced to its God, and would rather render it destined for wrath, taking the two nouns passively: the place had been devoted to a kind of madness, ceaselessly inflaming vengeance against itself. Gill puts the same thought as long-deferred purpose — the destruction had been resolved on and postponed while the provocation continued.

What follows Calvin reads as a diagnosis rather than a list. The nation had not offended in one particular but given itself over, omitting nothing calculated to provoke, so that a universal blot ran through every part of life. A body may carry a disease or two and still keep sound members; here nothing sound remained.

Turning the back and not the face draws out all four. Gill pictures what should have happened — a pupil facing his master, a subject facing his prince — and finds instead the hinder part presented, which is contempt and plain rudeness. Calvin sharpens it: to look away while someone speaks is a deliberate slight, seen by the speaker and meant to be seen, so the fall came by premeditated obstinacy and not ignorance; and since God shows his face whenever he prescribes duty or points the way of salvation, the refusal to look back is detestable pride. Ellicott observes that both this image and the phrase about rising early are favourites of the book. Clarke draws a quieter inference from that repetition — morning preaching, he supposes, must have been common in the country.

The pollution of the sanctuary is what ends hope, in Calvin's account. Private superstition was bad enough, incense on the housetops and libations poured to strangers; but when idols stood in the house that carried the divine name, repentance had no purchase left. He objects to the rendering that makes the name merely called there. The house had been dedicated, and to sacrifice in it to another was sacrilege rather than mere apostasy, a stripping of honour from its owner, and far more notorious than anything done indoors.

The valley below the city completes the exchange, becoming a rival sanctuary. Calvin recalls that sacrifice was restricted by the law to the one appointed place, so that carrying sons and daughters through fire elsewhere corrupted worship twice over. He notes that the same shrine is credited to one god in the earlier clause and another in the later, and concludes that the first name covers idols of every sort: the people meant to leave supreme sovereignty where it belonged while inventing patrons of their own, and that is how the gods multiplied. Gill takes the two names for one power and points to their meanings, master and king, as the proof.
36:
Calvin marks the hinge. Everything so far had established that the people deserved the worst — a land that should have been sacred polluted throughout, filth carried into the sanctuary, warnings long despised, and a God anxious for their safety whose kindness they proudly put out. Having settled that they had earned rejection outright, the oracle turns. What the besieged were saying, that the city was handed over, they meant as a verdict beyond appeal, and deliverance gave them no comfort because they held their case hopeless; the reply denies the finality, not the disaster.

The gathering answers a real difficulty. Calvin points out that a people driven to one place might imagine a return, but these were scattered piecemeal, which made the promise look incredible; so the exile is declared temporary and the dispersed are to be collected. Clarke notes only that the promise recurs often in this book. Gill reads it on two horizons — the end of the seventy years, and a fuller accomplishment later, when the nation is converted and brought back from a wider dispersion.

The covenant formula that follows is, for Calvin, the first of the blessings rather than one among them. Wealth and plenty would leave the condition unimproved if the people were not owned; no one is happy who lives on the goods of this frail life, and the psalm calls that nation blessed whose God is the Lord. Temporal benefits are tokens of a father's favour, but he will not have them lived on; they are steps raising the mind to the fountain of happiness itself. Gill calls the sentence a compact summary of the covenant of grace, the more striking because the verdict standing against them now is that they are not his people.

One heart and one way Gill expands into a portrait of what converted souls share, whatever their nation: the same sense of sin, the same abandonment of their own righteousness, the same recourse to Christ, the same promises, the same trials and so the same sympathy, and the same things written within — the law, the doctrine, the implanted graces of faith, hope, love, fear and humility, in a heart sincere and not double. Clarke adds two adjectives that do the work of an argument, a clean heart and a safe road, with one object of worship and one salvation, and calls the blessing a profitable inheritance running on to the children. Wesley reduces it to concord in judgment and worship by the given rule.

Ellicott sets the same words against the discords the prophet could see around him — some serving the Lord and some the idols of the valley, some urging surrender and some intriguing abroad — and finds promised a unity of faith that shows itself in unity of action. He does not pretend it has come. The hope reappears transfigured in the prayer that all may be one and in the apostolic wish that all be joined in one faith, and those prayers, he says plainly, are still waiting.

On the everlasting covenant the four diverge by distance. Calvin contrasts it with the covenant of the law, called new in the preceding chapter because the fathers fell away so soon and its doctrine was letter and death; its failure, he insists, was accidental, since the law would have held had anyone kept it, and the repetition here is meant to stop proud men robbing grace of its praise. Ellicott identifies the promised fear with the fear that begins wisdom, the lack of which had been the national curse, dread of punishment having proved no substitute. Gill pushes the covenant back before time, an eternal transaction concerning the elect that can never be superseded as the older one was. Wesley applies it to those who received Christ, unless a national conversion still unaccomplished is meant.
41:
That God should be said to take pleasure in doing good is, for Calvin, borrowed speech: fathers are glad when they can benefit their children, and the affection had no other way of being said. He then draws out a contrast most readers miss: there had been delight in the punishing too, since a right judgment satisfies its author; what changes is not that pleasure enters but which of the two is shown. Gill fills in the same delight from the other end, a love of complacency resting on the people as they stand in Christ rather than in themselves, expressed in acts rather than words — mercy shown, salvation worn like ornament, prosperity enjoyed by the giver, no good thing withheld until they are brought home. Clarke simply marvels at the condescension of a God waiting to give with his whole heart.

The planting is a stronger word than it looks. Calvin points out that a settlement had been made once already, when the land was parcelled out under the successor of Moses, and the psalm about a vine carried out of Egypt describes it; but that stock was torn up, so the centuries down to the exile were no plantation at all, the people never having struck firm root. What is promised here is therefore new, and its perpetuity is part of the promise. Ellicott takes the adverb rendered assuredly in its plain sense of in truth, and prefers to hear in it not a guarantee about the tenure but an oath about the one who guarantees, close in form and force to the verily of the Gospels.

Who the promise covers is where the readings part. Calvin restricts it: most of the nation was cast off for good, a small Church survived, and the words belong to the elect remnant rather than to all twelve tribes, as the apostle's use of them shows. He presses the point because hypocrites appropriate whatever is said to the faithful while merely borrowing the name, and because the purpose was to keep despair from blocking the road to prayer. Clarke will not have the account settled so early: nothing resembling this good arrived after the return from Babylon, and since the word cannot fail, a rest still remains for that people, to be had under the Christian dispensation.

The sign is then tied back to the doctrine. Calvin explains what signs are for — the teaching is authentic without them, but they are conceded to our weakness so that the promise may sit more firmly — and notes in passing that the despairing sentence about a land emptied of man and beast was never the language of the leading men, who answered the prophet with cruelty instead. Gill treats the purchase as pledge and earnest twice over, confirming both the literal repopulating and, since the smaller promise was honoured, the spiritual ones behind it; he records as well the reading that makes the singular field the field of the Church, bought at a greater price and first planted in that country.

The closing picture returns to the deed. Gill sees money plentiful enough to be put into ground that had lain long untilled, worked again for public and private good, and mentions those who take the buyers for congregations gathered by a profession worth more than silver. Clarke reads it strictly as the symbolic purchase made good, restoring not merely the territory but each family to its own inheritance, which nothing short of divine power could arrange. Calvin walks the boundaries listed — the tribal lot in which part of the city and one of its gates lay, the surrounding villages, the towns of the hills and the lowland, and the south reaching toward Egypt — and finds the reason attached: the captives come back, and possession follows them.
